steps.title: A bus on the move
steps.display: Motion tells you how position changes.
steps.narration: You watch a danfo pull away. It covers a little road at first, then more each second. That growing speed is the change we want to measure.

sources.where: Topics 2(b) and 3, Linear motion and projectiles

steps.title: Describe a journey and its changes
steps.display: average speed = \frac{distance}{time}; average velocity = \frac{displacement}{time}
working: a = \frac{v − u}{t} (m s^{−2}); speed and velocity in m s^{−1}
distance = 8 m; displacement = 0 m; t = 4 s
average speed = 2 m s^{−1}; average velocity = 0 m s^{−1}
steps.narration: To compare trips, you need to know whether direction matters. Walk four metres out and four back in four seconds. You averaged two metres per second for speed, but your average velocity was zero. You finished where you started.

sources.where: Topics 2(b) and 3, Linear motion and projectiles

steps.title: Choose one of the four constant-acceleration equations
steps.display: v = u + at; s = ut + \frac{1}{2}at^{2}
working: u, v in m s^{−1}; a in m s^{−2}; s in m; t in s
steps.narration: To avoid chasing an unnecessary number, pick the equation that leaves it out. Suppose you start at two metres per second. Gain one metre per second each second for two seconds. You finish at four metres per second. Notice how the starting speed still counts.

sources.where: Topics 2(b) and 3, Linear motion and projectiles

steps.title: Read slopes and areas on motion graphs
steps.display: distance–time slope = speed; position–time slope = velocity
working: velocity–time slope = acceleration (m s^{−2})
signed area under velocity–time graph = displacement (m)
area under speed–time graph = distance (m)
steps.narration: A graph can tell you more than a list of speeds. First check the axes so you know what the steepness means. At two metres per second for three seconds, the rectangle gives six metres. Its width is time, and its height is velocity.

sources.where: Topics 2(b) and 3, Linear motion and projectiles

steps.title: Treat free fall as downward acceleration
steps.display: upward positive ⇒ a = −g; downward positive ⇒ a = +g
working: g in m s^{−2}; neglect air resistance
steps.narration: You need a direction first because gravity keeps pulling the same way. Give a ball an upward speed of ten metres per second. With gravity at ten metres per second squared, it stops rising after one second. The pull is still there at that instant.

sources.where: Topics 2(b) and 3, Linear motion and projectiles

steps.title: Split projectile motion into two directions
steps.display: u_{x} = u cos θ; u_{y} = u sin θ; a_{x} = 0; a_{y} = −g
working: x = u_{x}t; y = u_{y}t − \frac{1}{2}gt^{2}; v_{y} = u_{y} − gt
Use the actual landing height y to find t when levels differ.
steps.narration: A flying ball moves sideways while gravity changes its upward motion. Split the motion so you can use the same clock for both. At three metres per second sideways, it covers six metres in two seconds.

sources.where: Topics 2(b) and 3, Linear motion and projectiles

steps.title: Find level-ground flight time, height and range
steps.display: T = \frac{2u sin θ}{g}; H = \frac{u^{2}sin^{2}θ}{2g}; R = \frac{u^{2}sin(2θ)}{g}
working: Same launch and landing height; T in s; H and R in m.
At the top v_{y} = 0, so t_{up} = \frac{u_{y}}{g}.
steps.narration: Check the landing level because going up and coming down take equal times only here. Start with an upward part of ten metres per second. With gravity at ten metres per second squared, it takes one second to reach the top. You can double that for the whole flight.

sources.where: Topics 2(b) and 3, Linear motion and projectiles

steps.title: Write the given quantities
steps.display: A stone is released from rest. How far does it fall in 2 s?
steps.narration: Before you choose a rule, look at how the stone starts. Released means nobody gives it a push, so it starts at rest. Take gravity as ten metres per second squared. Let down be positive because that is where the stone goes.

steps.title: Choose a rule without final speed
steps.display: s = ut + \frac{1}{2}at^{2}
steps.narration: We want the distance, so there is no need to find its ending speed. Pick the rule that uses the starting speed, gravity and time. See how the starting part drops out when you put in zero.

steps.title: Square the time and read the distance
steps.narration: The stone gets quicker during the fall, so the time appears twice in the distance calculation. Square the two seconds first, then take half of ten times four. You get twenty metres down from the release point.

steps.title: Identify the start and what is asked
steps.display: A car starts from rest and moves with a uniform acceleration of 30 m s^{−2} for 20 s. How far does it travel?
steps.narration: To choose the shortest route, mark the speed the car starts with. The words from rest tell you it starts at zero. We know how steadily it gains speed and for how long, so we can go straight to the distance.

steps.title: Use the time-squared term
steps.narration: The car spends the early part going slowly, so using its ending speed for the whole trip would double the distance. Keep the half in the rule. Twenty seconds squared gives four hundred seconds squared.

steps.title: Match metres to kilometres
steps.narration: The calculation uses metres, but the answers may be in kilometres. Each kilometre contains a thousand metres, so you divide by a thousand at the end. That gives six kilometres for the trip.

steps.title: Use zero as the final speed when stopping
steps.display: Wrong  t = 5 s; Right  t = 10 s
steps.narration: A train can still be moving even after losing some speed. Check what five seconds of braking actually removes. At two metres per second each second it loses only ten. You started at twenty, so you need another five seconds.

sources.where: Topics 2(b) and 3, Linear motion and projectiles

steps.title: Take the difference between both graph readings
steps.narration: To see how sharply it speeds up, compare the two readings on each axis. At the first point it is already moving. Take away the fifteen from the thirty five before you share that gain across ten seconds.

sources.where: Topics 2(b) and 3, Linear motion and projectiles

steps.title: Choose from the givens
steps.display: Choose directions and givens before the equation.
steps.narration: When you feel stuck, put a mark beside what you know. Then circle what you need. A direction convention and a rule that uses those givens will usually get you moving.

sources.where: Topics 2(b) and 3, Linear motion and projectiles

quickCheck.stem: Two bodies X and Y are projected on the same horizontal plane, with the same initial speed but at angles 30° and 60° respectively to the horizontal. Neglecting air resistance, the ratio of the range of X to that of Y is

options.why: For X, sin(2 × 30°) = sin 60°. For Y, sin(2 × 60°) = sin 120° = sin 60°. Since u and g are identical, R_{X} : R_{Y} = sin 60° : sin 120° = 1 : 1.
Range depends on sin 2θ, not directly on θ.
This uses cos θ rather than sin 2θ.
This uses sin θ rather than sin 2θ.

steps.title: A tray on the bus
steps.display: Changes in motion need a net force.
steps.narration: You hold a tray on a danfo. When the driver brakes, the tray wants to keep moving. You feel the push needed to slow it.

sources.where: Topics 3–5, Motion, Gravitational field and Equilibrium of forces

steps.title: Distinguish Newton’s three laws
steps.display: ΣF = 0 ⇒ v constant; ΣF = ma; F_{AB} = −F_{BA}
working: Net force in N; mass in kg; acceleration in m s^{−2}.
First law includes remaining at rest.
Third-law forces act on different bodies and are the same interaction.
steps.narration: Before you predict a change, follow one object. Two newtons each way on a tray leave it moving as before. Give one kilogram an unbalanced push of two newtons. Its velocity changes by two metres per second each second. A reaction push belongs to the other object.

sources.where: Topics 3–5, Motion, Gravitational field and Equilibrium of forces

steps.title: Distinguish mass and weight
steps.display: W = mg
working: W in N; m in kg; g in N kg^{−1} or m s^{−2}.
steps.narration: You need to tell how much matter you have from how hard gravity pulls it. Take a bag of two kilograms. Where gravity is ten newtons per kilogram, it weighs twenty newtons. The same bag could weigh less somewhere with weaker gravity.

sources.where: Topics 3–5, Motion, Gravitational field and Equilibrium of forces

steps.title: Connect impulse and momentum
steps.display: p = mv; J = Δp = F_{avg}Δt
working: p in kg m s^{−1}; J in N s.
Impulse is the signed area under a force–time graph.
F = 2 N; Δt = 3 s ⇒ J = 6 N s
steps.narration: A push can change motion a lot by lasting longer. Give a trolley a steady two newtons for three seconds. It gains six newton seconds of momentum in that direction. On a force graph, the area collects all those little pushes through time.

sources.where: Topics 3–5, Motion, Gravitational field and Equilibrium of forces

steps.title: Keep total momentum when external impulse is negligible
working: Use signed velocities; total momentum in kg m s^{−1}.
If they stick, v_{1} = v_{2} = v.
steps.narration: To follow a crash, look at the two objects together. One kilogram rolls at four metres per second and sticks to another kilogram at rest. They share the original momentum, so each moves at two metres per second. Their combined movement energy is smaller afterwards.

sources.where: Topics 3–5, Motion, Gravitational field and Equilibrium of forces

steps.title: Balance turning effects and forces
steps.display: moment = Fd_{⊥}; equilibrium ⇒ ΣF = 0 and Στ = 0
working: d_{⊥} is perpendicular distance from pivot to the line of action in m.
Moment in N m; clockwise and anticlockwise moments balance.
2 N × 3 m = 3 N × 2 m = 6 N m
steps.narration: A small push far from a hinge can turn as strongly as a bigger one nearby. Two newtons at three metres give the same turning effect as three newtons at two metres. For balance those turns must oppose each other. Also check for any leftover push.

sources.where: Topics 3–5, Motion, Gravitational field and Equilibrium of forces

steps.title: Find the inward change in circular motion
steps.display: v = rω; ω = \frac{2π}{T}; a_{c} = \frac{v^{2}}{r} = rω^{2}; F_{c} = ma_{c}
working: r in m; ω in rad s^{−1}; period T in s; a_{c} in m s^{−2}; F_{c} in N.
Centripetal force is the net inward force.
steps.narration: An object can speed round a bend without changing its speed. It still needs an inward push because its direction keeps changing. At two metres per second around a radius of two metres, the inward acceleration is two metres per second squared.

sources.where: Topics 3–5, Motion, Gravitational field and Equilibrium of forces

steps.title: Write down the mass and the pushes
steps.display: A 2 kg trolley is pushed right by 8 N and opposed by 2 N. Find its acceleration.
working: m = 2 kg; F_{right} = 8 N; F_{left} = 2 N; g = 10 m s^{−2}
steps.narration: You need the push that is left over before you know how the trolley moves. Start by making right positive. Take gravity as ten metres per second squared. The floor supports the trolley, so the vertical forces cancel.

steps.title: Combine the horizontal forces
steps.display: ΣF_{x} = 8 − 2 = 6 N to the right
steps.narration: One hand pushes the trolley along and the other push opposes it. You can see why eight newtons alone would predict too much acceleration. Subtract the opposing two. We now have six newtons left in the rightward direction.

steps.title: Share the net force over the mass
steps.display: a = \frac{6 N}{2 kg} = 3 m s^{−2} to the right
steps.narration: The same push changes a heavier trolley's speed more slowly. That is why we divide the net force by the mass here. Three metres per second squared means it gains three metres per second of rightward speed each second.

steps.title: Measure both distances from the pivot
steps.display: A 90 cm uniform lever has a load of 30 N suspended at 15 cm from one of its ends. If the fulcrum is at the centre of gravity, the force that must be applied at its other end to keep it in horizontal equilibrium is
working: length = 0.90 m; midpoint = 0.45 m; load position = 0.15 m
d_{load} = 0.30 m; d_{force} = 0.45 m
steps.narration: The turns depend on the pivot, so use it as your starting point for both distances. The middle is forty five centimetres from the end. The load sits fifteen centimetres from that end, leaving thirty centimetres between it and the pivot.

steps.title: Set the opposite moments equal
steps.narration: If one side turned harder, the lever would tip. The lever's own weight passes through the pivot, so it gives no turn there. The load turns it one way, and a downward push at the other end turns it back.

steps.title: Solve for the force at the far end
steps.narration: You need the same turning effect from a longer arm. That is why you should expect a smaller push than the load. Divide nine newton metres by the arm length. Twenty newtons at the far end balances it.

steps.title: Inertia applies to moving bodies too
steps.display: Wrong  inertia only opposes starting; Right  inertia resists any change in velocity.
steps.narration: If you only think about a stationary object, you miss half the idea. A moving tray needs a push to slow down just as a resting tray needs one to start. Ask what change is being resisted.

sources.where: Topics 3–5, Motion, Gravitational field and Equilibrium of forces

steps.title: Conserve momentum, not kinetic energy, in a sticking collision
steps.display: Wrong  K_{after} = 1000 J; Right  K_{after} = 50 J
steps.narration: Sticking is a clue that the objects move together after impact. Use their combined mass and the momentum they started with. That gives ten metres per second. Only then work out their motion energy, which is fifty joules.

sources.where: Topics 3–5, Motion, Gravitational field and Equilibrium of forces

steps.title: Draw the system first
steps.display: Name the system and choose a direction before balancing forces, moments or momentum.
steps.narration: When several objects are involved, draw a boundary around the ones you mean. Then choose a direction. You will see which pushes, turns and changes in motion belong in your calculation.

sources.where: Topics 3–5, Motion, Gravitational field and Equilibrium of forces

quickCheck.stem: An object moves along a circular path of radius 0.5 m at 1 m s^{−1}. What is its angular velocity?

options.why: 8 rad s^{−1} at this radius would give 4 m s^{−1}.
4 rad s^{−1} would give 2 m s^{−1}.
The relation v = rω gives ω = 1 ÷ 0.5 = 2 rad s^{−1}.
1 rad s^{−1} would give 0.5 m s^{−1}.

steps.title: A ramp at the market
steps.display: A smaller push can act over a longer distance.
steps.narration: You push a crate up a ramp. It feels easier than lifting straight up, but you travel farther. The ramp trades a smaller push for more distance.

sources.where: Topics 7–8, Work, Energy and Power and Simple Machines

steps.title: Count only force in the direction of motion
steps.display: W = Fs cos θ
working: F in N; s in m; W in J; θ between F and displacement.
Along: W = Fs; across: W = 0; opposite: W = −Fs.
2 N × 3 m = 6 J along the motion.
steps.narration: A pull can point partly away from where the crate moves. To count the part that helps, look at the angle between pull and travel. Two newtons straight ahead over three metres transfers six joules. A push across the direction gives zero work.

sources.where: Topics 7–8, Work, Energy and Power and Simple Machines

steps.title: Track energy of motion and height
steps.display: K = \frac{1}{2}mv^{2}; ΔU = mgΔh
working: K and U in J; m in kg; v in m s^{−1}; h in m.
For motion under gravity alone, K + U stays constant.
Friction transfers mechanical energy to internal energy; total energy is conserved.
steps.narration: You need two accounts when an object changes speed and height. A two kilogram trolley at two metres per second has four joules of movement energy. Double the speed, and it has sixteen. A lift instead adds energy through the change in vertical height.

sources.where: Topics 7–8, Work, Energy and Power and Simple Machines

steps.title: Compare how quickly energy is transferred
steps.display: P = \frac{W}{t} = \frac{E}{t}; 1 W = 1 J s^{−1}
working: P = Fv when force and velocity point the same way.
steps.narration: Two people can lift the same load and finish at different times. Power tells you who transferred the energy faster. If you do six joules of work in two seconds, that is three watts. Watch for minutes hiding in the question.

sources.where: Topics 7–8, Work, Energy and Power and Simple Machines

steps.title: Separate force gain, distance ratio and efficiency
steps.display: MA = \frac{load}{effort}; VR = \frac{effort distance}{load distance}; η = \frac{MA}{VR}
working: η = \frac{useful output work}{input work}; efficiency in percent = 100η
MA, VR and η have no units; ideal η = 1.
steps.narration: You can gain force by moving your hand farther than the load moves. If a two newton pull lifts six newtons, the force gain is three. Suppose your hand travels four times farther. Then three quarters of the input work reaches the load.

sources.where: Topics 7–8, Work, Energy and Power and Simple Machines

steps.title: Compare lever arms about the same pivot
steps.display: VR_{lever} = \frac{effort arm}{load arm}
working: Ideal perpendicular forces ⇒ effort × effort arm = load × load arm.
Use perpendicular moment arms; friction can reduce MA below VR.
2 m ÷ 1 m = 2; ideal effort for a 6 N load is 3 N.
steps.narration: A longer handle lets your hand move farther for the same turn. Put your hand two metres from the pivot and the load one metre away. Your hand moves twice as far for a small turn. An ideal lever then needs half the load force.

sources.where: Topics 7–8, Work, Energy and Power and Simple Machines

steps.title: Find velocity ratios for pulleys and ramps
steps.display: VR_{ideal pulley} = number of rope sections supporting the moving block; VR_{plane} = \frac{ramp length}{vertical rise}
working: A single fixed pulley changes direction and has VR = 1.
Two supporting rope sections ⇒ VR = 2.
A 4 m ramp rising 1 m gives VR = 4.
steps.narration: The machine helps because your end moves farther than the load. If two rope sections shorten together, pulling in four metres lifts the block two metres. For a ramp, compare the whole path with the rise. You use that same distance trade each time.

sources.where: Topics 7–8, Work, Energy and Power and Simple Machines

steps.title: Write the pump quantities
steps.display: A pump lifts 6 kg of water through 5 m in 3 s. Find its useful power.
steps.narration: First identify the useful job the pump does. It gives the water height, so you need mass, rise and time. Take gravity as ten metres per second squared. The question leaves the energy lost inside the pump out of this calculation.

steps.title: Find the useful work
working: mg = 60 N
steps.narration: You need the energy for the whole lift before you can find the rate. Gravity pulls on the water with sixty newtons. Lift against that pull for five metres, and you transfer three hundred joules to the water.

steps.title: Divide by the time for the lift
steps.narration: The three hundred joules describe the whole job. We need the amount per second, so spread that energy over the three seconds. You get one hundred watts of useful output for the lift.

steps.title: Read the lever’s distance ratio
steps.display: A lever of 90% efficiency lifts 180 N. Its effort arm is twice its load arm. Find the required effort.
steps.narration: You know how far each side moves compared with the other. For the same turn, the effort side travels twice as far. Write that ratio first. We will need the efficiency to find how much of the ideal force gain survives.

steps.title: Find the actual force gain
steps.narration: The lever loses some input work, so its force gain falls below two. Keep ninety per cent of the ideal ratio. The result, one point eight, tells you how many newtons of load each newton of effort can lift.

steps.title: Recover the effort force
steps.display: effort = \frac{180 N}{1.8} = 100 N
steps.narration: The load is the bigger force here, so divide it by the gain. You get one hundred newtons. Check the direction of the division by multiplying that effort by one point eight to recover the load.

steps.title: Use the angle measured from the displacement
steps.display: Wrong  W = 100 × 8 × sin 60°; Right  W = 100 × 8 × cos 60° = 400 J
steps.narration: Look at which way the crate travels before choosing sine or cosine. The rope angle starts from the horizontal path. The force part along that path is fifty newtons. That part contributes four hundred joules over eight metres.

sources.where: Topics 7–8, Work, Energy and Power and Simple Machines

steps.title: Use weight in a lifting calculation
steps.display: Wrong  P = \frac{mh}{t}; Right  P = \frac{mgh}{t}
steps.narration: A pump lifts against a pull measured in newtons. The question gives kilograms, so turn that mass into weight first. Otherwise the number loses the factor of ten in this question. You also need seconds for watts.

sources.where: Topics 7–8, Work, Energy and Power and Simple Machines

steps.title: Ask what changes and how fast
steps.display: Track where energy goes, then divide by time for power.
steps.narration: When a machine makes the job easier, ask what you trade for the smaller push. Then track the useful energy. If the question asks how fast that energy moves, bring in the time.

sources.where: Topics 7–8, Work, Energy and Power and Simple Machines

quickCheck.stem: At what height does an object have the same potential energy as an equal mass moving at 5 m/s? Use g = 10 m/s^{2}.

options.why: 25 is the square of the speed.
20 is the denominator 2g.
Equating mgh and \frac{mv^{2}}{2} gives h = \frac{25}{20} = 1.25 m, or 1.3 m to the choice precision.
1.0 m is too low.

steps.title: A foot on soft ground
steps.display: Pressure depends on force and contact area.
steps.narration: Stand on soft ground in flat sandals, then imagine the same weight on narrow heels. The heels sink farther because your weight presses on less ground.

sources.where: Topics 10–11, Pressure and Liquids at Rest

steps.title: Match force to area and mass to volume
steps.display: p = \frac{F_{⊥}}{A}; ρ = \frac{m}{V}; RD = \frac{ρ}{ρ_{water}}
working: p in Pa = N m^{−2}; ρ in kg m^{−3}; relative density has no unit.
For liquids and solids, use water as the reference.
steps.narration: A weight can press gently over a wide patch or hard on one spot. Put four newtons over two square metres and you get two pascals. To compare how tightly packed materials are, use mass and volume instead. You can compare that density with water.

sources.where: Topics 10–11, Pressure and Liquids at Rest

steps.title: Add the pressure from the fluid above a point
steps.display: p_{gauge} = ρgh; p_{absolute} = p_{surface} + ρgh
working: Static fluid of constant ρ; h is vertical depth in m.
h = 1 m ⇒ p_{gauge} = 10 000 Pa
steps.narration: A deeper point supports more liquid above it. That is why we measure depth from the surface. Take one metre of water and gravity at ten metres per second squared. The water adds ten thousand pascals. Add air pressure only when asked for the full pressure.

sources.where: Topics 10–11, Pressure and Liquids at Rest

steps.title: Read air pressure from a barometer
steps.display: p_{atm} = ρgh for a column with negligible pressure above it
working: Mercury barometer height is the vertical difference, with a near vacuum at the top.
Fixed ρ and g: 1 m → 2 m ⇒ pressure doubles.
steps.narration: Air pressure is hard to see, so let it hold up a liquid. Double the air pressure and a one metre column becomes two metres. A denser liquid needs a shorter column for the same pressure.

sources.where: Topics 10–11, Pressure and Liquids at Rest

steps.title: Pass on a pressure change through a fluid
steps.display: \frac{F_{1}}{A_{1}} = \frac{F_{2}}{A_{2}} for level pistons in an ideal hydraulic press
working: Pascal’s principle: applied pressure change is transmitted undiminished in an enclosed fluid.
A_{1}s_{1} = A_{2}s_{2} for incompressible fluid.
steps.narration: A narrow piston lets you create pressure with a small push. The enclosed liquid passes that change along. If the other piston has twice the area, a two newton push can produce four newtons there. The wider piston moves only half as far.

sources.where: Topics 10–11, Pressure and Liquids at Rest

steps.title: Find the upward force from displaced fluid
steps.display: F_{B} = ρ_{fluid}gV_{displaced}; W_{app} = W − F_{B}
working: F_{B}, W and W_{app} in N; V_{displaced} in m^{3}.
For a fully submerged object, V_{displaced} = V_{object}.
steps.narration: A submerged object makes room for liquid that used to be there. Weigh that missing liquid to find the upward push. If it would weigh two newtons and the object weighs five, a supporting scale shows three newtons. Keep the two weights separate.

sources.where: Topics 10–11, Pressure and Liquids at Rest

steps.title: Balance weight and upthrust for flotation
steps.display: F_{B} = W ⇒ \frac{V_{sub}}{V_{object}} = \frac{ρ_{object}}{ρ_{fluid}}
working: At rest, neglecting buoyancy of the air above the liquid.
ρ_{object} = 500 kg m^{−3}; ρ_{fluid} = 1000 kg m^{−3} ⇒ immersed fraction = \frac{1}{2}.
steps.narration: A floating object settles where the water pushes up just enough. A block with half the water's density needs only half its volume underwater. The other half can stay in air. Use the average density of the whole floating object.

sources.where: Topics 10–11, Pressure and Liquids at Rest

steps.title: Write the fluid quantities
steps.display: What gauge pressure acts 2 m below a water surface?
steps.narration: You want the extra push from water, so leave air pressure out for now. Note the depth and the density of the water. Take gravity as ten metres per second squared. We only need the water above the point.

steps.title: Find the weight per unit area
steps.display: p_{gauge} = ρgh = 1000 × 10 × 2 Pa
steps.narration: Imagine a narrow column of water reaching down to the point. A deeper column has more weight for the same base area. Multiply the density, gravity and depth to turn that weight per area into pressure.

steps.title: Report gauge pressure
steps.display: p_{gauge} = 20 000 Pa
steps.narration: The calculation gives twenty thousand pascals from the water. Keep that as the answer because the question asks for gauge pressure. If it asked for the whole pressure, you would add the pressure of the air above.

steps.title: Separate the two scale readings
steps.display: An object gives a scale reading equivalent to 22 kg when immersed in water and 30 kg when weighed in air. What upthrust does the liquid exert? Take g = 10 m s^{−2}.
working: m_{air equiv} = 30 kg; m_{water equiv} = 22 kg; g = 10 m s^{−2}
Δm_{equiv} = 8 kg
steps.narration: The change in the reading is the clue to the upward push. The scale gives two mass equivalents, so find the gap first. In water it reads eight kilograms less than in air. The force itself must be in newtons.

steps.title: Convert the reading gap into force
steps.display: F_{B} = Δm_{equiv}g = 8 × 10 = 80 N
steps.narration: The weight supported by the scale fell because the water helped hold the object up. Multiply that gap by the given gravity. The water supplies eighty newtons of support while the scale supplies the rest.

steps.title: Check against the apparent weight
steps.narration: Check by finding what each scale reading means as a force. The dry reading is three hundred newtons. The wet reading is two hundred and twenty. Their difference gives the same eighty newtons upward.

steps.title: Subtract buoyancy from the ordinary weight
steps.display: Wrong  W_{app} = 20 N; Right  W_{app} = 20 − 10 = 10 N
steps.narration: If a question says apparent, somebody is reading the support force in the liquid. The object's own weight is twenty newtons. Here the displaced liquid supplies ten newtons upward, so the scale only has to provide ten more.

sources.where: Topics 10–11, Pressure and Liquids at Rest

steps.title: Report the fraction below the surface
steps.display: Wrong  immersed fraction = 0.8; Right  immersed fraction = \frac{250}{1250} = 0.2
steps.narration: Before choosing between the two fractions, check which part the question wants. The piece is much less dense than the liquid, so only a fifth needs to sink. The other four fifths are the part you can see above the surface.

sources.where: Topics 10–11, Pressure and Liquids at Rest

steps.title: Identify the pressure or force being asked for
steps.display: Separate pressure at a point from the upward force on the whole object.
steps.narration: When you see water in a question, ask what you are measuring first. A point under the surface has pressure. An object feels an upward push from the fluid it displaces.

sources.where: Topics 10–11, Pressure and Liquids at Rest

quickCheck.stem: A balloon of volume 300 m^{3} is filled with hydrogen. If the density of air is 1.3 kg m^{−3}, find the upthrust on the balloon. Take g = 10 m s^{−2}.

options.why: 3000 N treats the air density as 1.0 kg m^{−3}.
3800 N is below the weight of the displaced air.
The upthrust equals the weight of 300 m^{3} of displaced air, 1.3 × 300 × 10 = 3900 N.
4200 N would require an air density of 1.4 kg m^{−3}.

steps.title: A hot cup in a cool hand
steps.display: Heat flows while there is a temperature difference.
steps.narration: You hold a cup of hot tea. Your hands warm and the cup cools. Something passes from the hotter cup into your cooler hands.

sources.where: Topics 12–15, Temperature, Quantity of Heat, Change of State and Thermal Expansion

steps.title: Convert Celsius and Kelvin and calibrate a linear scale
working: \frac{X − X_{ice}}{X_{steam} − X_{ice}} = \frac{T_{°C}}{100} for a linear thermometer at standard fixed points.
0 °C = 273.15 K; a change of 1 °C equals a change of 1 K.
steps.narration: The same temperature can get different numbers on different scales. Think of melting ice at zero Celsius. On the Kelvin scale it reads two hundred and seventy three point one five. A one degree Celsius rise is still a one kelvin rise.

sources.where: Topics 12–15, Temperature, Quantity of Heat, Change of State and Thermal Expansion

steps.title: Use linear expansion with a signed temperature change
steps.display: ΔL = αL_{0}ΔT; L = L_{0} + ΔL
working: ΔT = T_{final} − T_{initial}; α in K^{−1}.
steps.narration: You want the small change before adding it to the old length. Take a one metre strip with a coefficient of one millionth per kelvin. Warm it by two kelvins. You add two millionths of a metre. Cooling would take length away instead.

sources.where: Topics 12–15, Temperature, Quantity of Heat, Change of State and Thermal Expansion

steps.title: Allow for expansion in two or three directions
steps.display: ΔA = βA_{0}ΔT; ΔV = γV_{0}ΔT; β ≈ 2α; γ ≈ 3α
working: Small expansion of an isotropic solid; β and γ in K^{−1}.
steps.narration: Look at how many directions each measurement can grow. For a solid that expands equally each way, try one part per million. That is about two parts in area and three in volume. Keep those coefficients separate.

sources.where: Topics 12–15, Temperature, Quantity of Heat, Change of State and Thermal Expansion

steps.title: Calculate heating without a change of state
steps.display: Q = mcΔT; C = mc
working: c in J kg^{−1} K^{−1}; C in J K^{−1}; Q in J.
steps.narration: Different materials need different amounts of energy for the same warming. Think of one kilogram that needs two joules per kilogram per kelvin. Warm it by three kelvins and it takes six joules. A larger sample needs more energy for the same rise.

sources.where: Topics 12–15, Temperature, Quantity of Heat, Change of State and Thermal Expansion

steps.title: Use latent heat during a change of state
steps.display: |Q| = mL; fusion = solid ↔ liquid; vaporisation = liquid ↔ gas
working: At the transition temperature for a pure substance at fixed pressure.
L in J kg^{−1}; Q in J.
steps.narration: A melting solid can absorb energy while the thermometer sits still. The energy helps it change state. If one kilogram needs three hundred joules to melt, two kilograms need six hundred. When that liquid freezes again, it gives this energy back.

sources.where: Topics 12–15, Temperature, Quantity of Heat, Change of State and Thermal Expansion

steps.title: Balance heat lost and gained in a mixture
steps.display: ΣQ = 0 for an isolated system
working: C_{hot}(T_{hot} − T_{f}) = C_{cold}(T_{f} − T_{cold}) for no phase change and negligible container heat.
Include the calorimeter and any phase change if they absorb or release energy.
steps.narration: You need to know where the heat from the hotter part goes. Mix equal masses of the same liquid at twenty and forty Celsius. With no losses or phase change, they meet at thirty. One cools by as much as the other warms.

sources.where: Topics 12–15, Temperature, Quantity of Heat, Change of State and Thermal Expansion

steps.title: Write the masses and temperatures
steps.display: Mix 1 kg of water at 20 °C with 3 kg at 40 °C. Find the final temperature with no heat loss.
working: m_{cold} = 1 kg; m_{hot} = 3 kg; T_{cold} = 20 °C; T_{hot} = 40 °C
g = 10 m s^{−2}; same c; container heat negligible.
steps.narration: The larger portion can give more heat for each degree it cools. That tells you the answer should be closer to forty. Take gravity as ten metres per second squared for our setup. Gravity does not enter this heat balance.

steps.title: Write the energy balance
steps.narration: The warm water's lost energy goes into the cooler water. Both sides involve the same material, so the specific heat capacity cancels. The masses still matter. See how the three on the warm side gives it more weight in the balance.

steps.title: Solve and check the temperature
steps.narration: You can check whether the result makes sense by testing both changes. The larger portion cools by five degrees, while the smaller one warms by fifteen. Three times five matches fifteen. The final temperature falls between the two starting temperatures.

steps.title: Find the signed temperature change
steps.display: A wire is 100.0 m long at 30°C. Its linear expansivity is 2 × 10^{−5} K^{−1}. What is its length at −10°C?
steps.narration: Before finding the length, decide whether the wire warms or cools. It goes from thirty Celsius to ten below zero. That is a drop of forty degrees. The wire should therefore end up a little shorter.

steps.title: Calculate the small change
steps.narration: The expansion coefficient describes a fraction of the original length for each degree. Multiply by the whole starting length and the signed temperature change. The minus sign in the result tells you the wire shrank.

steps.title: Give the length rather than the change
steps.narration: The question asks for how long the wire is at the end. So apply that small decrease to the original hundred metres. You get ninety nine point nine two metres, slightly under the starting length as expected.

steps.title: Keep the temperature fixed during melting
steps.display: Wrong  melting pure ice at 0 °C requires a temperature rise; Right  melting absorbs latent heat at 0 °C.
steps.narration: A steady thermometer can make it look as if no energy is going in. Look at what the ice is doing instead. It changes into liquid while the temperature holds. The mass stays the same, and this particular change reduces the volume.

sources.where: Topics 12–15, Temperature, Quantity of Heat, Change of State and Thermal Expansion

steps.title: Use three times the coefficient for volume
steps.display: Wrong  γ = α; Right  γ ≈ 3α for small isotropic expansion.
steps.narration: The brass piece grows in three directions when it warms. The question only gives the change per direction. For a small expansion, count that contribution three times before finding the volume. Using it once would give only a third of the change.

sources.where: Topics 12–15, Temperature, Quantity of Heat, Change of State and Thermal Expansion

steps.title: Identify what the energy changes
steps.display: Use temperature change for heating and latent heat for a change of state.
steps.narration: Before choosing an equation, see what the energy is changing. The thermometer may move, or the material may melt or boil. If both happen in a question, treat them as separate stages.

sources.where: Topics 12–15, Temperature, Quantity of Heat, Change of State and Thermal Expansion

quickCheck.stem: Find the temperature rise when 500 J warms 100 g of water. Use c = 4200 J kg^{-1} K^{-1}.

options.why: 12.1°C is an order of magnitude too high.
2.1°C would require about 882 J.
Using Q = mcΔT with 0.100 kg gives ΔT = \frac{500}{420} ≈ 1.2°C.
0.1°C would require only about 42 J.

steps.title: A ripple along a rope
steps.display: A disturbance travels while each part oscillates locally.
steps.narration: You flick one end of a rope. The wiggle runs along it, but your end stays in your hand. Sound also carries a disturbance along.

sources.where: Topics 20–22, Waves, Propagation and Characteristics of Sound Waves

steps.title: Identify how the medium moves
steps.display: transverse: vibration ⟂ travel; longitudinal: vibration ∥ travel
working: Sound in air has compressions and rarefactions.
Mechanical waves need a medium; the disturbance carries energy.
Two flicks of a rope launch two pulses while each section moves across the direction of travel.
steps.narration: To tell wave types apart, watch one small bit of the medium. Give a rope two quick flicks and watch the pulses travel forward. Each bit moves across the path. In sound travelling through air, the bits move back and forth along the path instead.

sources.where: Topics 20–22, Waves, Propagation and Characteristics of Sound Waves

steps.title: Link wave speed, period and wavelength
steps.display: v = fλ; T = \frac{1}{f}
working: v in m s^{−1}; f in Hz; λ in m; T in s.
Amplitude is maximum displacement from equilibrium, in m for a displacement wave.
Successive crests or compressions are λ apart; adjacent compression and rarefaction are \frac{λ}{2} apart.
steps.narration: You can find how fast a pattern travels by counting passing waves. Say two waves pass each second and each is three metres long. The pattern advances six metres each second. The wait between crests is half a second.

sources.where: Topics 20–22, Waves, Propagation and Characteristics of Sound Waves

steps.title: Allow for the return journey in an echo
steps.display: d = \frac{vt}{2} for a reflected pulse returning to its source
working: Sound reflects at surfaces; multiple overlapping reflections cause reverberation.
steps.narration: An echo stopwatch runs all the way out and back. If a pulse covers six hundred metres in that time, the wall is three hundred metres away. One clear return is an echo. Many overlapping returns make the sound linger.

sources.where: Topics 20–22, Waves, Propagation and Characteristics of Sound Waves

steps.title: Match the natural patterns of strings and pipes
steps.display: f_{n} = \frac{nv}{2L} for fixed strings and open–open pipes; f_{n} = \frac{nv}{4L} for open–closed pipes, n odd
working: Fixed string ends and closed pipe ends: displacement nodes; open pipe ends: displacement antinodes.
Resonance is a large response when driving frequency matches a natural frequency.
Neglect end corrections; L in m; f in Hz; n = 1, 3, 5, … for open–closed.
L = 1 m; v = 320 m s^{−1} ⇒ f_{1} = 80 Hz for open–closed.
steps.narration: A string or pipe responds strongly when a repeating push fits one of its patterns. The end conditions tell you which patterns fit. A pipe one metre long with one closed end fits a four metre fundamental wave. The closed end cannot move freely.

sources.where: Topics 20–22, Waves, Propagation and Characteristics of Sound Waves

steps.title: Predict how the string’s pitch changes
steps.display: v = \sqrt{\frac{F_{tension}}{μ}}; f_{1} = \frac{1}{2L}\sqrt{\frac{F_{tension}}{μ}}
working: F_{tension} in N; μ is mass per length in kg m^{−1}.
Same L and μ: 4 N → 16 N ⇒ f changes from 100 Hz to 200 Hz.
steps.narration: You can raise a string's note by stretching it tighter. A tighter string carries the wave faster. Raise the tension from four newtons to sixteen. Keep the length and string the same. The frequency only doubles. Watch for the square root in that change.

sources.where: Topics 20–22, Waves, Propagation and Characteristics of Sound Waves

steps.title: Listen for the shift from motion
steps.display: approach ⇒ higher observed f; separation ⇒ lower observed f
working: Doppler effect changes observed frequency; wave speed in the stationary medium stays fixed.
Pitch follows frequency; larger amplitude raises intensity under otherwise fixed conditions.
Illustration: 2 crests per second → 3 crests per second received during approach.
steps.narration: A passing okada can sound higher before it reaches you. Imagine two successive crests leaving a moving source. The second starts closer to you while it approaches, so the gaps ahead shrink. If you receive three crests a second instead of two, the note sounds higher.

sources.where: Topics 20–22, Waves, Propagation and Characteristics of Sound Waves

steps.title: Write the echo time and speed
steps.display: A shout returns from a wall in 2 s. Sound travels at 340 m s^{−1}. Find the distance to the wall.
steps.narration: The question wants a one way distance, so notice what the stopwatch actually times. It starts at the shout and stops at the return. We take gravity as ten metres per second squared in the setup. The echo calculation uses sound speed instead.

steps.title: Find the whole sound path
steps.narration: You know how far the sound travels each second. Multiply by the time it spends on both legs. That gives six hundred and eighty metres of travel. See that we have counted the route towards the wall and back.

steps.title: Keep just the outward leg
steps.narration: The wall stays in one place, so the two legs are equal in this setup. Split the total into two equal parts. The wall is three hundred and forty metres away from the person who shouted.

steps.title: Identify the pipe’s two ends
steps.display: A pipe of length 45 cm is closed at one end. Calculate the fundamental frequency of the sound wave generated in the pipe if the velocity of sound in air is 360 m/s. [Neglect end corrections]
working: L = 0.45 m; v = 360 m s^{−1}; one end closed
steps.narration: Start with the ends because they tell you what shape the air can make. The closed end holds the air still there. At the opening, the air can swing back and forth freely. That gives you a quarter of a wavelength in the pipe.

steps.title: Find the full wavelength
steps.narration: You only have the shortest piece of the wave that fits between these two ends. Four such lengths make a complete wave. Use metres for the pipe length and you get one point eight metres for the wavelength.

steps.title: Turn wavelength into frequency
steps.narration: The speed tells how many metres the pattern moves each second. Each wave takes up one point eight metres, so divide to count how many waves pass per second. You get two hundred hertz.

steps.title: Treat echo time as a round trip
steps.display: Wrong  depth = 1500 × 4 = 6000 m; Right  depth = 3000 m
steps.narration: The clock keeps running after the sound hits the seabed. If you use all four seconds for the way down, you count the return leg again. Take half the distance, or use two seconds for the outward leg.

sources.where: Topics 20–22, Waves, Propagation and Characteristics of Sound Waves

steps.title: Use matching points for a full wavelength
steps.display: Wrong  λ = 0.17 m; Right  λ = 0.34 m and f = 1000 Hz
steps.narration: A compression and a neighbouring rarefaction show opposite parts of the pattern. Look for the next compression to complete the wave. Doubling the given gap gives zero point three four metres. Then divide the speed by that full wavelength.

sources.where: Topics 20–22, Waves, Propagation and Characteristics of Sound Waves

steps.title: Spot a complete cycle first
steps.display: Identify what repeats and how far or how long it takes.
steps.narration: When a wave question gives you a gap or a time, check what that measurement covers. It could be a whole wave or just part of one. Then choose the relation that fits.

sources.where: Topics 20–22, Waves, Propagation and Characteristics of Sound Waves

quickCheck.stem: In a closed organ pipe producing a musical note, an antinode will always be produced at

options.why: The rigid closed end prevents displacement of the air.
The midpoint is not always an antinode.
At the open end the air can oscillate with a large displacement, so it is a displacement antinode. The closed end is a displacement node.

options.text: all the parts of the pipe
options.why: A standing wave has separate nodes and antinodes.

steps.title: A spoon at the table
steps.display: Shape changes where reflected or refracted rays meet.
steps.narration: Look into the bowl of a shiny spoon. Your face can turn upside down as it moves away. The curved surface sends light back in different directions.

sources.where: Topics 24–25, Reflection and Refraction of Light

steps.title: Measure reflection angles from the normal
steps.display: i = r; the incident ray, reflected ray and normal lie in one plane
working: Normal is perpendicular to the surface.
Plane mirror: virtual, upright, same size; image as far behind as object is in front.
i = 30° ⇒ r = 30°; approach along the normal ⇒ i = r = 0°.
steps.narration: You need one steady line to compare incoming and outgoing light. Draw it at a right angle where the ray hits. A ray thirty degrees from that line leaves thirty degrees on the other side. The mirror surface gives a different angle.

sources.where: Topics 24–25, Reflection and Refraction of Light

steps.title: Classify images using the focal point
steps.display: For spherical mirrors near the axis: |f| = \frac{R}{2}
working: Concave mirror and convex lens converge; convex mirror and concave lens diverge.
For a real object at u > f, a converging device gives a real inverted image; u < f gives a virtual upright enlarged image.
At u = f the outgoing rays are parallel; diverging devices give virtual upright reduced images for real objects.
steps.narration: A screen can catch light only where the rays themselves meet. If a concave mirror has a radius of two metres, parallel rays meet one metre away. Bring your face closer than that point. Then the rays spread, and you see an upright virtual image.

sources.where: Topics 24–25, Reflection and Refraction of Light

steps.title: Use one sign convention for mirrors and lenses
steps.display: \frac{1}{f} = \frac{1}{u} + \frac{1}{v}; M = \frac{h_{i}}{h_{o}} = −\frac{v}{u}
working: Real-is-positive: u > 0 for real objects; v > 0 for real images and v < 0 for virtual images.
f > 0 for converging devices; f < 0 for diverging ones. u, v, f in m; M has no unit.
Real image is in front of a mirror but beyond a lens for a real object.
steps.narration: You need signs because the same formula handles real and virtual images. Start a real object two metres from a converging device of focal length one metre. The image forms two metres away. The minus in the magnification tells you it is upside down.

sources.where: Topics 24–25, Reflection and Refraction of Light

steps.title: Use Snell’s law at a boundary
steps.display: n = \frac{c}{v}; n_{1}sin i = n_{2}sin r
working: Refractive index n is dimensionless; c and v in m s^{−1}. Angles are measured from the normal.
Incident ray, refracted ray and normal share a plane.
steps.narration: A ray can bend because it changes speed at a boundary. If light travels at half its vacuum speed in a material, the index is two. When a slanting ray enters it from air, the ray bends closer to the normal.

sources.where: Topics 24–25, Reflection and Refraction of Light

steps.title: Check the direction before using the critical angle
steps.display: sin C = \frac{n_{2}}{n_{1}} when n_{1} > n_{2}
working: At i = C, r = 90°; at i > C, total internal reflection.
steps.narration: At some boundaries, all the light can bounce back. Check that it is heading towards a lower index first. At the limiting angle, it skims the boundary. From an index of two into air, that angle is thirty degrees. A larger angle gives total internal reflection.

sources.where: Topics 24–25, Reflection and Refraction of Light

steps.title: Find apparent depth for near-normal viewing
steps.display: \frac{real depth}{apparent depth} ≈ \frac{n_{object medium}}{n_{observer medium}}
working: Use near-normal rays at a plane interface; depths in m.
From air, apparent depth ≈ real depth ÷ n.
n = 2; real depth = 2 m ⇒ apparent depth ≈ 1 m.
steps.narration: A submerged object can look closer because your eye traces bent rays back in straight lines. Look almost straight down through a liquid of index two from air. Something two metres below the surface then looks about one metre below it.

sources.where: Topics 24–25, Reflection and Refraction of Light

steps.title: Write the object and focal distances
steps.display: A convex lens has focal length 0.10 m. An object is 0.20 m away. Find the image distance and magnification.
steps.narration: We need the image position and its size compared with the object. Mark the lens as converging and the object as real. Take gravity as ten metres per second squared in this setup. It does not enter the ray calculation.

steps.title: Isolate the image term
steps.narration: The two distances enter as reciprocals, so start by finding one over the image distance. The focal term gives ten per metre. The object term takes away five per metre. Turn what remains upside down to get the distance.

steps.title: Use the sign to read the image
steps.narration: The positive distance puts the real image on the far side of the lens. The size ratio has magnitude one, so the image matches the object's size. Its minus sign tells you the top becomes the bottom.

steps.title: Use real-image signs
steps.display: If a convex lens of focal length 12 cm is used to produce a real image four times the size of the object, how far from the lens must the object be placed?
steps.narration: The word real tells you where the rays meet, so choose a positive image distance. The image size is four times the object size. That means the image distance is four times the object distance in this sign convention.

steps.title: Combine the distance terms
steps.narration: You can use one unknown because both distances are tied together. A whole reciprocal and a quarter reciprocal make five quarters. Use that to turn the equation into a direct statement about the object distance.

steps.title: Check position and image size
steps.narration: You get fifteen centimetres, just beyond the focal point. That fits a real, enlarged image on the far side. Its distance is sixty centimetres from the lens. The negative magnification confirms the image is upside down.

steps.title: Put a shaving face inside the focus
steps.display: Wrong  f < u < 2f for an upright enlarged image; Right  0 < u < f.
steps.narration: An enlarged face still needs to look upright when you shave. Between the focus and the centre of curvature, the rays meet and turn the image upside down. Move your face inside the focus to see the enlarged upright version.

sources.where: Topics 24–25, Reflection and Refraction of Light

steps.title: Do not infer magnification from apparent distance
steps.display: Wrong  plane mirror M > 1; Right  plane mirror M = +1.
working: Image and object heights match. The image is virtual and upright.
steps.narration: The image looks as though it is behind the glass, but that does not stretch it. The plane mirror places it as far back as you stand in front. Its height stays the same, so the size ratio is one.

sources.where: Topics 24–25, Reflection and Refraction of Light

steps.title: Follow the rays before choosing signs
steps.display: Use the ray path to decide what the image signs and angles mean.
steps.narration: When an optics answer looks odd, sketch where the light actually goes. You can see whether rays meet or only appear to meet. That picture helps you choose both the angle and the sign.

sources.where: Topics 24–25, Reflection and Refraction of Light

quickCheck.stem: A submarine is observed to rise from a real depth of 80 m to 60 m in water. Calculate the change in apparent depth. [Refractive index of water = \frac{4}{3}]

options.why: 60 m is the apparent depth when the submarine is at 80 m real depth.
At 80 m real depth, apparent depth = 80 × \frac{3}{4} = 60 m. At 60 m real depth, apparent depth = 60 × \frac{3}{4} = 45 m. Change in apparent depth = 60 − 45 = 15 m.
80 m is the initial real depth.
45 m is the apparent depth when the submarine is at 60 m real depth.

steps.title: Paths through a junction
steps.display: Follow the routes available to charge.
steps.narration: You are at a junction with two open roads. People can split between them and meet again later. An electrical circuit can offer charge more than one route.

sources.where: Topics 30–31, Electric Cells and Current Electricity

steps.title: Distinguish charge flow from energy per charge
steps.display: I = \frac{Q}{t}; V = \frac{E}{Q}
working: Q in C; t in s; I in A; E in J; potential difference in V.
Q = 2 C; t = 1 s; E = 6 J ⇒ I = 2 A; V = 3 V.
steps.narration: You need two measurements to describe what a circuit does. Two coulombs passing in one second make two amps. If those charges transfer six joules, each coulomb transfers three joules. That makes three volts. One number describes flow, the other energy per charge.

sources.where: Topics 30–31, Electric Cells and Current Electricity

steps.title: Apply Ohm’s law under steady conditions
steps.display: V = IR for an ohmic conductor at fixed temperature
working: R in Ω; V in V; I in A.
Slope on a V against I graph gives R for an ohmic conductor.
At fixed R = 2 Ω: 8 V gives 4 A.
steps.narration: To predict the flow, see how much the path resists it. Four volts across two ohms drive two amps. Keep the temperature fixed. If twice the voltage gives twice the current, you have what we call an ohmic conductor.

sources.where: Topics 30–31, Electric Cells and Current Electricity

steps.title: Add resistances along one path
working: Current is the same through each; individual potential differences add.
steps.narration: A series path gives charge no choice about where to go. Each resistor gets the same current, so each adds its own voltage drop. Put two ohms and three ohms in that one path. Together they behave like five ohms.

sources.where: Topics 30–31, Electric Cells and Current Electricity

steps.title: Add reciprocal resistances across shared terminals
steps.display: \frac{1}{R_{parallel}} = \frac{1}{R_{1}} + \frac{1}{R_{2}} + …
working: Branch voltages are equal; branch currents add.
Equivalent resistance is below the smallest finite positive branch resistance.
2 Ω in parallel with 2 Ω gives 1 Ω.
steps.narration: Another branch gives charge another way across. Each branch sees the same voltage, but each carries its own current. Two equal branches of two ohms together behave like one ohm. Notice how adding a path reduces the resistance.

sources.where: Topics 30–31, Electric Cells and Current Electricity

steps.title: Allow for the resistance inside a cell
steps.display: V_{terminal} = ℰ − Ir; I = \frac{ℰ}{R+r} when the cell supplies a load
working: E.m.f. is energy supplied per charge; ℰ and V_{terminal} in V; r and R in Ω.
Open circuit: I = 0 ⇒ V_{terminal} = ℰ.
ℰ = 6 V; I = 1 A; r = 2 Ω ⇒ V_{terminal} = 4 V.
steps.narration: A cell can lose some of its push inside itself once charge flows. Suppose its open circuit reading is six volts. One amp through two ohms inside the cell costs two volts. You then measure four volts across the outside terminals.

sources.where: Topics 30–31, Electric Cells and Current Electricity

steps.title: Relate a wire’s dimensions to its resistance
steps.display: R = \frac{ρL}{A}
working: ρ is material resistivity in Ω m; L in m; A in m^{2}.
Same ρ and L: doubling A halves R.
Same ρ and A: doubling L changes 2 Ω to 4 Ω.
steps.narration: A longer wire gives charge a longer path through the material. Widen the wire and you give it more room. If a wire is two ohms, twice the length with the same cross section gives four ohms. Hold the material and temperature fixed.

sources.where: Topics 30–31, Electric Cells and Current Electricity

steps.title: Write the cell and resistor values
steps.display: A 6 V cell has internal resistance 1 Ω and supplies a 2 Ω resistor. Find terminal voltage.
steps.narration: We need the voltage that reaches the outside resistor. Some of the cell's push is used inside it whenever current flows. Write down both resistances first. Take gravity as ten metres per second squared for this setup, though it plays no part in the circuit.

steps.title: Use the whole loop to get current
steps.display: I = \frac{6 V}{1 Ω + 2 Ω} = 2 A
steps.narration: The current must pass through the cell's internal resistance and the external resistor in the same loop. Add them before dividing. Six volts across that three ohm path drives two amps through both parts.

steps.title: Find the drop across the load
steps.display: V_{terminal} = IR = 2 × 2 V = 4 V
steps.narration: The terminals are on either side of the outside resistor, so work out its share of the voltage. That gives four volts. The other two volts are lost inside the cell, which checks the full six.

steps.title: Choose a connection that lowers resistance
steps.display: A circuit has a resistance of 200 Ω. The resistance of the circuit can be reduced to 120 Ω when
working: R_{old} = 200 Ω; R_{target} = 120 Ω ⇒ use parallel.
steps.narration: First check whether the target is above or below the starting resistance. We want less than two hundred ohms, so we need to give charge another path. A positive resistor placed along the same route would increase the total.

steps.title: Isolate the reciprocal of the new resistance
working: R_{new} = 300 Ω
steps.narration: The parallel rule adds the contributions from each branch. Subtract the original branch's contribution from the combined one. You now have one over the new resistance. Make sure you turn that result back over.

steps.title: Check the combination
steps.narration: To check, put three hundred ohms alongside the original two hundred. The combined value comes out at one hundred and twenty ohms. It is smaller than either branch, which is what we expect with an extra path.

steps.title: Find the current in the requested branch
steps.display: Wrong  use total current; Right  I_{12 Ω} = \frac{12 V}{12 Ω} = 1 A
steps.narration: Look at which wire the question points to before doing any arithmetic. Each branch sees the battery's twelve volts. To find the current in the twelve ohm branch, use just that branch's resistance. The other branches carry their own currents.

sources.where: Topics 30–31, Electric Cells and Current Electricity

steps.title: Recognise an unloaded e.m.f. measurement
steps.display: Wrong  a fixed resistance ratio makes it accurate; Right  at balance I_{test cell} = 0 and V_{terminal} = ℰ.
steps.narration: An instrument can change the voltage it is trying to measure if it draws current. At the balance point, the test cell supplies none. That means there is no lost voltage inside it, so the measurement gives its full e.m.f.

sources.where: Topics 30–31, Electric Cells and Current Electricity

steps.title: Trace the path before calculating
steps.display: One path means shared current, and shared terminals mean shared voltage.
steps.narration: Before you add anything, follow the wires with your finger. Decide whether charge has one way through or different branches to choose from. Then you can see which currents or voltages must match.

sources.where: Topics 30–31, Electric Cells and Current Electricity

quickCheck.stem: Three resistors, 2 Ω, 4 Ω and 12 Ω are connected in parallel and a 12 V battery is connected across the combination. The current flowing through the 12 Ω resistor is

options.why: 3.2 A does not equal \frac{12 V}{12 Ω}.
9.6 A is close to total circuit current (10 A), not the 12 Ω branch current.
14.4 A multiplies 12 by 1.2 wrongly.
Since the resistors are in parallel, the p.d. across the 12 Ω resistor is the full 12 V. Therefore I_{12} = \frac{V}{R} = \frac{12}{12} = 1.0 A.

steps.title: Lights on the meter
steps.display: Total energy depends on power and time.
steps.narration: You leave a light on while cooking. A brighter lamp can use energy faster, but even a small lamp adds to the bill if it stays on.

steps.title: Use voltage and current to find input power
steps.display: P = IV
working: P in W, I in A, V in V; 1 W = 1 J s^{−1}.
steps.narration: Two appliances can use the same voltage and draw different currents. To compare how fast they take in energy, you need both numbers. Two amps at three volts takes in six watts. That means six joules enter the device each second.

steps.title: Choose the resistor form that fits the givens
steps.display: P = I^{2}R = \frac{V^{2}}{R} for a resistor
working: Use V across and I through the same resistor.
I = 2 A; R = 3 Ω; V = 6 V ⇒ P = 12 W by either formula.
steps.narration: You can work out heating without knowing both the current and voltage. For two amps in a three ohm resistor, square the two first. Four times three gives twelve watts. At the same resistance, doubling the current makes four times the heat per second.

steps.title: Use matched units for energy
working: W × s gives J; kW × h gives kWh.
steps.narration: The meter keeps counting as long as the appliance runs. Five watts for two seconds transfers ten joules. For a bill, you would use kilowatts and hours instead. Notice that a kilowatt hour measures energy, even though its name contains a power unit.

steps.title: Add the energies and apply the tariff
steps.display: cost = (ΣP_{kW}t_{h}) × tariff per kWh
working: For a common operating time, add powers first.
2 × 1 kW × 1 h = 2 kWh; at ₦3/kWh, cost = ₦6.
steps.narration: A meter adds what each appliance uses during its running time. Take two heaters of one kilowatt each for one hour. Together they use two units. At three naira per unit, that energy costs six naira. Use separate times if the appliances ran for different lengths.

steps.title: Use ratings to estimate normal current
steps.display: I_{rated} = \frac{P_{rated}}{V_{rated}}; fuse in series with live conductor
working: A fuse melts on sustained excess current; choose a suitable rated fuse according to equipment and circuit protection requirements.
Opening live disconnects supply to the appliance; a neutral-only fuse can leave it live.
steps.narration: A fuse needs to carry the ordinary current but stop an unsafe excess. A ten watt load on five volts draws two amps. A fuse marked two amps is not an exact trip threshold. Look for the specified suitable rating above normal current in exam questions.

steps.title: Write the appliance rating and time
steps.display: An 80 W lamp runs for 5 s. Find the energy transferred.
steps.narration: You need the whole amount of energy, so start with how fast it transfers and how long it runs. Take gravity as ten metres per second squared for this setup. It is the lamp's rating and running time that matter here.

steps.title: Treat each second as another share
steps.narration: The lamp transfers eighty joules each second at its rated power. Count five equal shares of that energy. Look at the units as you multiply. The seconds in the time and the per second in power cancel each other.

steps.title: Read the answer in joules
steps.narration: The question asks how much energy moved, so finish in joules. Five shares of eighty make four hundred. If the same lamp ran for ten seconds, the energy would double while its power rating would stay the same.

steps.title: Add the running powers
steps.display: Five 50 W and four 100 W lamps run for 10 h. How much does the energy cost at 2 kobo per kWh?
steps.narration: The lamps all run for the same time, so you can add their powers before working out the energy. The small lamps together draw two hundred and fifty watts. The large ones draw four hundred. Keep both groups in that total.

steps.title: Match energy units to the tariff
steps.narration: The price is for a kilowatt hour, so use kilowatts with the ten hours. The lamps use a little over half a unit each hour. After ten hours that is six and a half units altogether.

steps.title: Multiply by the cost per unit
steps.display: cost = 6.5 kWh × 2 kobo/kWh = 13 kobo = ₦0.13
steps.narration: Now you have something the tariff can price. Pay two kobo for each of those six and a half units. That is thirteen kobo. There are a hundred kobo in a naira, so the answer is thirteen hundredths of a naira.

steps.title: Change hours to seconds when the answer is in joules
steps.display: Wrong  E = 60 J; Right  E = 60 W × 3600 s = 216 000 J.
steps.narration: Watts count joules each second, so one hour must become seconds before you multiply. There are three thousand six hundred seconds. Keep the sixty watts and the same running time. The larger number comes from switching time units.

steps.title: Break the live supply to isolate an appliance
steps.display: Wrong  a neutral-only fuse isolates the appliance; Right  a fuse in live disconnects the live feed.
steps.narration: You want the faulty appliance cut off from the supply voltage. A break in neutral stops current round the loop, but parts can stay connected to live. In the exam diagram, look for protection on the live side.

steps.title: Keep power, energy and cost distinct
steps.display: Use power and time to find energy before multiplying by a tariff.
steps.narration: When a question looks like a bill, ask which quantity the number describes. Watts tell you the rate. The time turns it into energy. Then the price per unit tells you the charge.

quickCheck.stem: A 40 W instrument has a resistance of 90 Ω. On what voltage should it be operated normally?

options.why: 150 V would dissipate \frac{150^{2}}{90} = 250 W.
225 V would exceed the 40 W rating many times over.
3600 is V^{2} = P R, before taking the square root.

steps.title: Half the pile again
steps.display: A half-life halves the amount still undecayed.
steps.narration: Imagine a pile of beans. Set half aside each round and keep playing with the rest. The same fraction goes each round, even when the pile gets smaller.

steps.title: Identify alpha, beta and gamma
working: Alpha is a helium nucleus; beta-minus is an electron emitted in nuclear decay; gamma is a photon.
Alpha is strongly ionising and weakly penetrating. Beta penetrates farther. Gamma is generally the most penetrating and least directly ionising of these three.
One α carries away 2 protons and 2 neutrons, for a total of 4 nucleons.
steps.narration: You need to know what left before working out what remains. In an alpha particle, count two protons and two neutrons. That gives four particles from the nucleus. A beta minus particle is an electron. Gamma carries energy away without taking protons or neutrons.

steps.title: Balance both numbers in a nuclear equation
steps.display: ΣA_{before} = ΣA_{after}; ΣZ_{before} = ΣZ_{after}
working: A counts nucleons; Z identifies proton number of a nucleus.
α: A − 4 and Z − 2; β^{−}: A unchanged and Z + 1; γ: both unchanged.
In β^{−} emission, a neutron becomes a proton, electron and antineutrino.
steps.narration: Checking both rows helps you avoid losing track of the nucleus. Take one alpha away and the top number drops by four. The bottom drops by two. In the example, add those small counts back to check that both rows balance.

steps.title: Count halvings of what remains
working: n = \frac{t}{T_{1/2}}; remaining fraction = (\frac{1}{2})^{n}; decayed fraction = 1 − (\frac{1}{2})^{n}.
t and T_{1/2} must use the same time unit.
8 → 4 → 2 after two half-lives (expected counts).
steps.narration: The next interval acts only on the part still there. Start with eight undecayed nuclei in a simple model. One half life leaves four on average. A second leaves two. You halve the new amount each time, so equal times remove unequal amounts.

steps.title: Connect half-life, decay constant and activity
steps.display: T_{1/2} = \frac{ln 2}{λ}; A_{activity} = λN; N = N_{0}e^{−λt}
working: λ in s^{−1}; activity in Bq = s^{−1}; T_{1/2} in s.
Subtract constant background from measured count rate before applying the half-life rule. Count rate is not necessarily activity.
8 Bq → 4 Bq after T_{1/2}.
steps.narration: To compare samples, you may need the rate of decay now. It falls as the number of undecayed nuclei falls. A source at eight becquerels drops to four after one half life. If you measure it with a counter, remove the background reading first.

steps.title: Match uses and protection to penetration
steps.display: Medical tracers can be detected outside the body; ionising radiation requires controlled exposure.
working: Uses include tracers, radiotherapy and thickness monitoring.
Reduce exposure time, increase distance and use appropriate shielding under radiation protection procedures.
Same dose rate: 2 s gives half the dose of 4 s.
steps.narration: You need radiation to reach the detector in a tracer study. That same ability to travel is why protection matters. If an exposure lasts two seconds instead of four at the same dose rate, it gives half the dose. Distance and suitable shielding help too.

steps.title: Write the half-life and time
steps.display: A sample starts at 80 Bq. Its half-life is 2 h. Find its activity after 6 h.
steps.narration: The question asks for the rate that remains, so we can count how many times it halves. Both times use hours already. Take gravity as ten metres per second squared in the setup. Radioactive decay here depends on the given half life.

steps.title: Find how many half-lives fit
steps.narration: You want to know how many equal intervals fit into the wait. Divide the whole time by one half life. The seconds cancel, leaving three. That number tells you how many times to cut the remaining rate in half.

steps.title: Halve the remaining activity three times
steps.display: 80 Bq → 40 Bq → 20 Bq → 10 Bq
steps.narration: Each arrow starts from the rate left after the previous step. Half of eighty is forty, then half of forty is twenty. The third cut leaves ten becquerels. We have used each of the three intervals once.

steps.title: Start with the parent and list the emissions
steps.display: The radioisotope ^{235}_{92}U decays by emitting two alpha particles, three beta particles and a gamma ray. What are the mass and atomic numbers of the resulting daughter element?
working: A = 235; Z = 92; emissions: 2α, 3β^{−}, γ
steps.narration: The question wants two different numbers in a particular order. Start by separating the total particles in the nucleus from just the protons. Treat the unqualified beta particles as beta minus in this past question. Now follow the two counts separately.

steps.title: Subtract what the alphas carry away
steps.narration: An alpha takes protons and neutrons out together. Each carries four particles altogether, including two protons. Taking out two alphas removes eight from the total, and four from the proton count. Keep the results in those separate columns.

steps.title: Apply beta minus and gamma changes
steps.narration: A beta minus emission changes a neutron into a proton. Three such changes raise the proton count to ninety one. The total stays at two hundred and twenty seven. Gamma gives off energy, so neither number moves again.

steps.title: Check how many times you must halve
steps.narration: One half life only gets you halfway down the first step. Look at the starting one thousand and stop when you reach one hundred and twenty five. It takes three cuts in half, and each takes twenty seconds.

steps.title: Check the proposed interval against the remaining fraction
steps.display: Wrong  T_{1/2} = 10 years; Right  T_{1/2} = 120 ÷ 6 = 20 years.
steps.narration: Before dividing the total time, count how many halvings give one sixty fourth. Six does it because two to the sixth is sixty four. A ten year answer would give twelve halvings in this question, leaving far less.

steps.title: Separate what changes from what remains
steps.display: Track the two nuclear counts separately, and halve only the undecayed amount.
steps.narration: First ask whether the question wants the identity of a nucleus or the size of a sample. For identity, follow both counts. For the sample left, keep applying each half life to what remains.

quickCheck.stem: A radioactive substance has a half-life of 20 days. What fraction of the original radioactive nuclei will remain after 80 days?

options.why: Number of half-lives n = \frac{80}{20} = 4. Fraction remaining = (\frac{1}{2})^{4} = \frac{1}{16}.
\frac{1}{8} is the fraction left after 3 half-lives (60 days), not 80 days.
\frac{1}{4} is the fraction left after 2 half-lives (40 days).
\frac{1}{32} is the fraction left after 5 half-lives (100 days).
